title: Himself as subject
hook: I am myself the matter of my book, he tells the reader

segments.voice: Yesterday, quoting and changing: Montaigne added to his book but didn't correct it. Your line was keep adding. Which old page got a new line? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-eight.

The first page of Montaigne's book does not invite you in. It tells you to stop reading. Before the first essay, he puts a short note headed To the reader. It's a book of good faith, he says. He wrote it for his family and friends, so that after they lose him, they can find some trace of him again. And then the last lines: I am myself the matter of my book. You'd be unreasonable, reader, to spend your free time on a subject so slight and so vain. So, farewell. Today, a very strange welcome for a book.
screen: `A NOTE: TO THE READER.` → `FOR FAMILY AND FRIENDS.` → `SO, FAREWELL.`

segments.voice: First, who the book was for. Montaigne says he had no thought of serving the reader, or of his own glory. He wrote so that the people who knew him could keep something of him after he died. Second, how he wanted to be seen. If he'd wanted the world's favor, he says, he'd have dressed himself up. Instead he wants to be seen in his simple, natural, ordinary way, without strain or artifice, because it's himself he's painting. His faults will be there to read. Third, the subject. I am myself the matter of my book. Not kings, not wars, not the nature of the universe, though he touches all of those. One ordinary man, looked at honestly from the inside. Then the joke: why would you waste your time on that? Farewell. Of course the reader doesn't leave. Fourth, what writing himself did to him. In a later essay he turns it around: I have no more made my book than my book has made me. Painting himself for others, he says, he painted his inside in clearer colors than he had before. The writing changed the writer. You don't need to publish anything for this to work. Describing yourself honestly, even in one paragraph nobody reads, can show you to yourself in clearer colors. The subject is always available. It's you.
screen: `FOR FAMILY AND FRIENDS.` · `SIMPLE, NATURAL, ORDINARY.` · `I AM THE MATTER OF MY BOOK.` · `MY BOOK HAS MADE ME.` · then, large: `MYSELF THE MATTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: compose one honest paragraph about yourself, first in your head. Sit, and breathe. Begin the way Montaigne might: simply, naturally, without dressing up. One thing you like. One thing you're bad at. One habit you'd rather nobody noticed. One thing you hope people remember. Say it plainly, not to impress anyone. After the bell, if you like, write it down. The bell holds the time.
Himself as subject. Montaigne tells the reader, in his opening note, that he is himself the matter of his book, painted in his simple, ordinary way. Today's word.
Your line: myself the matter. Today, write one honest paragraph about yourself, for nobody but you, faults included. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Montaigne's Essays open with a short note to the reader saying the book was written for his family and friends, and that he himself is its subject, painted plainly, faults and all.

who he says the book was for

myth: Montaigne's opening note urges the reader to keep going
it calls the subject slight and vain and ends: so, farewell.
he says he wrote for his family and friends
so they could find some trace of him after losing him.
he says the writing changed him
I have no more made my book than my book has made me.

fork.setup: you're Montaigne, writing the note at the front of your book. if you wanted the world's favor, what would you do?
options: show your simple, ordinary self, faults included.
fork.reveal: he says that if he'd wanted favor he'd have dressed up; instead he paints himself plainly, faults and all.

trapdoor: what you thought: writing about yourself is vanity.
what it means: Montaigne wrote himself plainly so the people who knew him could keep something of him, and the writing showed him to himself.
what a scholar hears: the joke in the note's last lines, calling the subject too slight to read and saying farewell, sits alongside his later claim that the book made him as much as he made it.

notes: Montaigne paraphrased throughout. 'I am myself the matter of my book' is close to the usual English rendering but is not cited to a listed translation; treated as paraphrase.
